City of Burnaby · Council term 2022–2026

How each Councillor voted

Independent summary, not affiliated with the City of Burnaby. Every Council vote from November 2022 to August 2026, rebuilt from the City of Burnaby's official meeting minutes (110 meetings). Burnaby doesn't publish a voting table, so each vote was read from the minutes, which name anyone who opposed. Routine motions such as adopting the agenda or adjourning are left out.

Summary

Key findings

  • Burnaby's Council is the most consensual of the five. 93% of votes (2,230 of 2,393) were unanimous, and only 163 were split.
  • Mayor Mike Hurley rarely dissents (24 “no” votes) and is on the winning side 88% of the time. He votes most closely with Joe Keithley (90% agreement on split votes).
  • Maita Santiago, Daniel Tetrault and Alison Gu form the tightest group (85–92% agreement). Santiago and Tetrault are on the winning side of nearly every split vote (89–94%).
  • Richard T. Lee is the most frequent dissenter (81 “no” votes) and was the only “no” 41 times, more than all other members combined. Most of his solo votes are against budgets, financial plan bylaws and utility rates. He is on the losing side of nearly half of split votes.
  • Sav Dhaliwal and Pietro Calendino often vote together (77% agreement). Dhaliwal was the only “no” 17 times, including on drinking in parks and FIFA event planning.
  • Housing policy produced the closest votes. The first inclusionary rental requirements were rejected 7–2 in March 2025; a revised version passed the next month. Transit-oriented area designations passed 5–4 in May 2024 with Hurley, Dhaliwal, Keithley and Lee opposed. A 2026 motion on Brentwood Park restrictive covenants and small-scale housing failed 5–4.
  • Attendance. Mayor Hurley missed 17 meetings; Lee missed almost none. Absent members aren't counted in the “against” rates.

How each member votes, by category

Categories are assigned from keywords in each motion's title and text, since Burnaby's minutes don't tag topics. Each cell shows "no" votes out of votes cast in that category. Darker cells mean a higher share of "no" votes. A vote can belong to more than one category: a rezoning for a six-storey rental building counts under both Housing & density and Development. Method

How to read this

Source. The City of Burnaby's Council meeting minutes: 110 sets of City Council, Special Council and Inaugural minutes from 2 November 2022 to 25 August 2026, retrieved 29 September 2026. Each vote links to its minutes and, where available, the meeting video.

How votes were counted. Burnaby records each result as “CARRIED UNANIMOUSLY”, “CARRIED” or “DEFEATED”, followed by the names of anyone opposed. Members named as opposed are counted against; everyone else present is counted for. Attendance comes from each meeting's present and absent lists, adjusted when a member declared a conflict of interest and left, or joined late.

“Against” means against that motion. Referrals, amendments and motions to reject something are separate votes, and a “no” on them can mean support for the underlying item. Expand any row to read the motion.

Limits. Four sets of minutes from 2022–2023 are scanned images, so their text was read with character recognition and may contain small errors. When a member stepped out briefly and returned, the minutes don't say which votes they missed, so they're counted as present. Each reading of a bylaw is its own vote. Some main motions voted after an amendment have no separate text in the minutes and are marked as such.

Categories. Each vote is sorted by keywords in its title and motion text. A vote can sit in several categories, and some placements are judgment calls.

Privacy. Names of residents who spoke at meetings are removed from the motion text here.
